name: High-temperature and industrial heat pumps
summary: Industrial heat pumps upgrade low-grade waste heat into useful hot water or steam, reducing the fuel needed for process heating.
useCase: A food plant recovers refrigeration heat and uses it to pasteurise or clean equipment instead of producing all its heat with gas.
whyNow: High-temperature products are moving from prototypes into operating industrial sites. The IEA’s 2026 review says systems below 120°C have entered commercial operation and units below 160°C are beginning to do so. Japan’s installed industrial capacity approached 650 MW in 2024, but this still served only around 1% of light-industry heat demand. Wider adoption depends on each site’s waste-heat temperature, operating hours, electrical connection and electricity-to-gas price ratio. A good coefficient of performance in one demonstration is not a universal economic case: the required temperature lift is decisive. This is a market with strong technical potential and highly uneven project economics.

mainstream.scope: Routine selection for suitable low-to-medium-temperature process-heat projects in food, paper and other light industries, especially with recoverable waste heat.
mainstream.rationale: Repeat industrial packages, integrator experience and rising efficiency support adoption in the early 2030s. This does not imply widespread replacement of very high-temperature furnaces. IEA’s current-policy scenario is broadly stagnant through 2035, whereas its stated-policy scenario reaches about 8% of light-industry heat demand; policy and electricity economics are therefore material conditions.

metric.name: Installed industrial heat-pump capacity in Japan
metric.scope: Japan; industrial equipment only, not residential or all commercial heat pumps.
metric.limitations: Only one comparable observation within 2021–2026 was publicly established in the selected sources. The IEA/HPT commentary gives 290 MW a decade earlier, but that lies outside the requested five-year window. Do not invent annual values or infer the industrial trend from residential sales.
metric.futureNote: No defensible comparable external deployment forecast found. The separate maturity path is an analyst scenario, not measured adoption.
metric.growthLabel: ≈650 MW in Japan in 2024; sparse annual data

milestones.text: The IEA HPT Annex 58 programme began its 2021–2023 high-temperature heat-pump work; deployment statistics remained fragmented.
IEA HPT’s synthesis describes demonstration of equipment reaching around 120°C during this period.
Annex 58 published its technology review in September, consolidating available products and development work.
Japan’s industrial heat-pump capacity reached nearly 650 MW, still about 1% of light-industry heat demand.
EHPA’s industrial programme highlighted operating use in food, paper, chemicals and other industries; this is sector evidence, not a global installation census.
IEA’s first Heat Pump Monitor identified early commercial operation below 160°C and major policy-dependent differences in the 2035 outlook.

tailwinds: Reusing waste heat can reduce fuel use and exposure to fossil-fuel price volatility.
Existing compressor, refrigeration and engineering suppliers can industrialise proven components.
Long operating hours in factories can improve payback when electricity is competitively priced.
bottlenecks: Capital cost, process integration and plant downtime complicate retrofits.
High electricity-to-gas prices can outweigh an attractive technical efficiency.
Above roughly 160–200°C, technology readiness and economics remain more demanding.
watchMetrics: MW thermal commissioned for industrial service, separated by delivered temperature.
Measured seasonal/process COP and total delivered heat cost at a specified temperature lift.
Share of repeat orders and standard packages versus heavily customised pilots.
